purpose: This vaccine helps protect you against a serious bacterial infection called meningococcal disease caused by group B bacteria. This infection can lead to life-threatening meningitis (swelling of the brain and spinal cord) and bloodstream infections. Getting vaccinated is one of the best ways to protect yourself from this dangerous illness.
how_it_works: This vaccine contains small pieces of a protein called factor H binding protein (fHbp) that is found on the surface of the meningococcal B bacteria. When you receive the shot, your immune system learns to recognize these proteins and builds a defense against them. If you are ever exposed to the real bacteria in the future, your immune system will be ready to fight it off quickly.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site, which is very normal. You may also feel tired, have a headache, muscle aches, chills, or a mild fever for a day or two after the shot. These reactions are signs that your immune system is working and usually go away on their own.
warnings: Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you have ever had a severe allergic reaction to a previous meningococcal vaccine or to any of the vaccine ingredients. If you develop signs of a serious allergic reaction such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a rapid heartbeat after the shot, seek emergency help right away. This vaccine is not recommended if you are currently very sick with a high fever; it is better to wait until you feel better. Fainting can sometimes occur after any vaccine, so you may be asked to sit or lie down for 15 minutes after your shot.
typical_dosing: This vaccine is given as a shot into the muscle, usually in the upper arm. For most people, it is given as a 2-dose series, with the second dose given about 6 months after the first. In certain high-risk situations, a 3-dose series may be recommended at 0, 1 to 2, and 6 months. Your doctor will let you know the schedule that is right for you.
